title: Radioactive Decay Law and Half-Life

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 12 — Nuclei

explanation: Radioactive decay follows a first-order exponential law: the number of undecayed nuclei N decreases exponentially with time, governed by the decay constant λ (probability of decay per unit time, characteristic of each radioactive isotope). Half-life T½ (time for exactly half the initial nuclei to decay) is related to λ by T½ = 0.693/λ, and — crucially — is INDEPENDENT of the amount of substance present, a defining feature of this first-order-like process. Activity A = λN is the number of decays per unit time, decreasing over time exactly as N does.

variables.meaning: Number of undecayed nuclei at time t

workedExample.scenario: A radioactive sample with half-life 10 days starts with N₀ nuclei; find the fraction remaining after 30 days.
workedExample.result: 1/8 of the original nuclei remain after 30 days

commonMistakes: Assuming half-life changes depending on how much sample is present — half-life is a fixed, constant property of the isotope, entirely independent of the initial quantity.
Using linear (rather than exponential) reasoning for decay over multiple half-lives — after n half-lives, the fraction remaining is (1/2)ⁿ, not a simple linear fraction.
genZNote: Half-life doesn't care how much you started with — same isotope, same fixed decay clock, every time.
